title: Extending the Staggered-Start Pilot
text:
Riverton Distribution Center tested staggered start times for eight weeks after supervisors reported long truck queues and crowded employee entrances at 7:00 a.m. Under the pilot, half of the morning warehouse crew began at 6:30, while the rest began at 7:15. Operations manager Elena Park recommends continuing the staggered schedule for six more months while the center collects data across busier and slower seasons. She argues that the pilot reduced loading-area congestion, improved employee punctuality, and did so without meaningfully reducing productivity or changing the center's basic staffing level.

The clearest evidence concerns congestion. Before the pilot, 38 percent of inbound trucks arriving between 6:45 and 7:30 waited more than fifteen minutes before reaching an open bay. During the eight-week pilot, that share fell to 17 percent. Supervisors also counted an average of twenty-six vehicles in the entrance queue at 7:05 before the change, compared with fourteen during the pilot. Park says those measures matter because the schedule was designed to spread the morning arrival rush rather than increase the number of loading bays.

Park also points to employee punctuality. During the eight weeks before the pilot, 11.8 percent of morning clock-ins were more than five minutes late. During the staggered schedule, the rate was 6.4 percent. A follow-up survey found that some employees on the 7:15 start said they could use a later public-bus connection instead of paying for a ride when they missed the earlier bus. However, Park does not use the survey alone as proof of improved punctuality; the clock-in records are the direct measure of whether workers arrived on time.

Productivity data are less dramatic but still important to Park's recommendation. The center processed 21.4 orders per labor hour during the eight weeks before the pilot and 21.1 during the pilot. The number of damaged-order reports also remained nearly unchanged. Park interprets those results cautiously: the staggered schedule did not increase output, but the center appears to have reduced congestion and lateness without a large productivity loss. She therefore rejects the claim that the pilot succeeded because it made employees work faster.

The pilot has limits. It took place during a relatively steady shipping period, not the holiday peak, and employees could request which start time they preferred. A construction project on a nearby road also ended during the third week, which may have reduced some traffic outside the facility. Park says these factors are reasons to keep measuring rather than reasons to discard the pilot. A six-month extension would let the center compare results across heavier demand and less favorable travel conditions. If truck waiting and late clock-ins remain lower while productivity stays close to its previous level, Park argues, the evidence would be strong enough to consider making staggered starts permanent.
